{"id": "102:1/q15", "question": "What did Ubayy report about the saying on Adam's desire for wealth?", "turns_on": "The reports vary in valley count and in whether they describe prior treatment of the saying as Qurʾān or only its admonitory content.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q15/p1", "position": "People had treated the saying as Qurʾān until this sūra was revealed.", "reasons": "Versions mention one or two valleys of gold, desire for another, a belly filled only by earth, and divine acceptance of repentance. Ibn al-ʿArabī calls the report sound and neglected by commentators. Ibn ʿĀshūr says 'we' could mean Muslims generally and does not fix a Medinan date."}, {"id": "102:1/q15/p2", "position": "The saying belongs to the broader prophetic warning against endless acquisition.", "reasons": "Anas's version asks for a second valley after a first, while Ubayy's variations ask for a third; Study Quran cites it as a parallel to takāthur."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q16", "question": "Does this sūra establish punishment in the grave?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q16/p1", "position": "Yes: ʿAlī says uncertainty about grave punishment ended when this passage was revealed.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās takes the verse as indicating grave punishment; ʿAlī's report is transmitted by al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Durr, al-Suyūṭī, and Ibn Kathīr. Ibn Kathīr cites al-Tirmidhī's gharīb judgment; al-Itqān and al-Ālūsī also use the report in dating the sūra."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q17", "question": "Was the sūra revealed in Mecca or Medina?", "turns_on": "The rival Quraysh and Ansari occasion reports, Ubayy's wording, ʿAlī's grave-punishment report, and the fit of the sūra's threats to a Meccan audience.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q17/p1", "position": "It is Meccan.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says he knows no disagreement; Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān report exegetical consensus, while recording al-Bukhārī's contrary label. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers Mecca because the severe warning suits polytheists and the Quraysh occasion; he rejects Ubayy's 'we' as proof of Medina, since it could mean Muslims generally. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ and Asad call it early Meccan."}, {"id": "102:1/q17/p2", "position": "It is Medinan.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says Medina in Jishumī; al-Bukhārī is cited against the exegetes by Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān. Al-Suyūṭī and al-Ālūsī prefer Medina, using the Ansari occasion; al-Ālūsī adds Ubayy's saying and ʿAlī's grave-punishment report, arguing the latter is mentioned in Medinan material. Ibn ʿĀshūr contests Ubayy's dating inference."}, {"id": "102:1/q17/p3", "position": "Its place of revelation is disputed.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī states the dispute without choosing."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q18", "question": "What names are reported for the sūra?", "turns_on": "The reported companion title differs between al-Mughīra and al-Maqbara; codices also vary between two opening-word titles.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q18/p1", "position": "Al-Takāthur is the common title; some codices and al-Bukhārī call it Alhākum.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites most codices, commentaries, Tirmidhī, and old Qayrawan codices for the first title."}, {"id": "102:1/q18/p2", "position": "Some Companions called it al-Mughīra.", "reasons": "Saʿīd b. Abī Hilāl transmits this name through Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Durr."}, {"id": "102:1/q18/p3", "position": "Some Companions called it al-Maqbara, the Graveyard Sūra.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr both attribute this to Saʿīd b. Abī Hilāl, although other transmissions here give al-Mughīra."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q19", "question": "How many verses does the sūra have and where is it placed in revelation order?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q19/p1", "position": "It has eight verses.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says this is unanimous; several sūra headings agree."}, {"id": "102:1/q19/p2", "position": "On the Meccan chronology, it is sixteenth, after al-Kawthar and before al-Māʿūn.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives both neighbors; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ calls sixteenth a common dating and names al-Kawthar; Study Quran places it after al-Kawthar."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q20", "question": "What merit or recitation practice is reported for this sūra?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different merits and circumstances; the weeping promise is explicitly graded weak.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q20/p1", "position": "Reciting it counts like reciting a thousand verses.", "reasons": "Reports from Ubayy, Ibn ʿUmar, and ʿUmar give the merit; Ibn al-Milq suggests its teaching of return to God is one of six Qurʾānic aims and matches one sixth of roughly 6,200 verses, but al-Ālūsī says the true basis lies beyond that calculation."}, {"id": "102:1/q20/p2", "position": "A report promises Paradise to whoever weeps at its recitation, or feigns tears.", "reasons": "Al-Durr records the invitation and repeats the promise at a second recitation; al-Bayhaqī weakens the report."}, {"id": "102:1/q20/p3", "position": "The Prophet recited the sūra in prayer or in a companion's hearing.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Shikhkhīr says he found the Prophet reciting it, including one version in prayer through its end."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q21", "question": "How does al-Takāthur connect with al-Qāriʿah and nearby sūras?", "turns_on": "The proposed al-Qāriʿah link is either thematic in the canonical order or also treated as a direct sequential explanation; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ disputes chronological succession.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q21/p1", "position": "It follows al-Qāriʿah's account of the Hour by naming the worldly rivalry that causes ruin and distracts from preparing for it.", "reasons": "Jishumī says the preceding chapter ended with disbelievers in Hell; al-Biqāʿī says this sūra identifies their cause of misery, and Ibn al-Zubayr says rivalry in kin and numbers diverts from al-Qāriʿah's terrors. Islāḥī pairs the two around the afterlife's scale of good deeds versus worldly treasure."}, {"id": "102:1/q21/p2", "position": "The link to al-Qāriʿah is thematic in muṣḥaf order, not a chronological succession.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports al-Nīsābūrī's link but rejects chronological succession because Takāthur precedes Qāriʿah by thirteen sūras in revelation; she allows shared warning tone."}, {"id": "102:1/q21/p3", "position": "The following al-ʿAṣr recalls time wasted by striving for increase.", "reasons": "Study Quran says time is one of the blessings for which people will be questioned, connecting 102:1 and 102:8 with the following sūra."}, {"id": "102:1/q21/p4", "position": "An extended sequence links accumulation to slander, mockery, and the pride associated with the Elephant.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Zubayr, as cited by al-Biqāʿī, connects 102:1, 104:1, and 105:1."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q22", "question": "What is the proper lesson and practice of visiting graves in relation to this rebuke?", "turns_on": "Whether literal visitation serves remembrance and reform or becomes the very boastful practice condemned by the passage.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q22/p1", "position": "A grave visit should awaken reflection on death and judgment, prayer to God, and resolve for good deeds.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cites the hadith that visiting graves reminds of the afterlife. He describes greeting the dead, praying to Allah for living and dead, reciting Qurʾān and dedicating reward, and reflecting on resurrection, scales and destinations (101:4–11); he compares a visit to reading a book and learning from the deceased's good example. Ibn ʿĀbidīn says benefit varies with visitors' insight."}, {"id": "102:1/q22/p2", "position": "Using graves to boast of ancestors defeats their lesson and is rebuked.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says the dead's deeds are theirs and ours ours (2:141), so competing over them is pointless. Love of the good should follow God and the Prophet (2:165, 3:31); a person rises with those loved, but worship and aid are sought from Allah, not the dead. He prefers reading the passage as rebuke rather than encouragement of literal visiting."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q23", "question": "How does the opening warning return at the sūra's end?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q23/p1", "position": "Questioning over blessings exposes the cost of indulgence and calls for gratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says even lawful pleasure is restrained by knowing the majestic King will question it, more so disliked or forbidden pleasure. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says ingratitude leads to loss and punishment; Study Quran says verses 3–8 promise certain knowledge of Hellfire."}, {"id": "102:1/q23/p2", "position": "The warning can be illustrated through five ordinary blessings.", "reasons": "The Ibn ʿAbbās report in al-Thaʿlabī names a full stomach, cold drink, sleep, shade, and sound constitution after discussing wrongful accumulation, graves, and judgment."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q24", "question": "What does the sūra's basmala contribute to its theme?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q24/p1", "position": "It presents divine majesty, general provision and guidance, and completed mercy for those God loves.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī gives this reading in both transmitted segments."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q25", "question": "How does takāthur relate to God's nature?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q25/p1", "position": "Increase and decrease do not apply to God, whom no number or place circumscribes.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says God's holy name precedes time and cannot be spatially limited; the incapacity of number to encompass Him excludes numerical change."}]}
{"id": "102:1/q26", "question": "What other uses of the l-h-w word family are noted?", "turns_on": "These are distinct lexical uses of related forms, rather than competing glosses of the verse's verb.", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q26/p1", "position": "The root is illustrated by stopping a conversation when thunder is heard.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and Ibn al-Jawzī tell this of Ibn al-Zubayr; Rāzī names al-Zubayr and gloss

{"id": "102:1/q27", "question": "What unrelated lexical gloss is preserved with these notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:1/q27/p1", "position": "Kāda means 'nearly' or 'came close'.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī refers to his earlier discussion of verbs; the note supplies no connection to the verse's vocabulary."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q01", "question": "What does ḥattā make the endpoint of the rivalry?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥattā limits the duration of distraction or the extent of what rivals count, and whether a grave visit itself changes them.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q01/p1", "position": "The distraction continues through life and ends only at death and burial.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn makes ḥattā the limit of alhākum; Ibn ʿĀshūr says no further action follows death. Elmalılı says death ends competition; Qatada's tribes die off one by one. Zayd b. Aslam transmits in a mursal report the Prophet's explanation that rivalry distracts until death arrives and people visit the graves."}, {"id": "102:2/q01/p2", "position": "The rivalry extends even to counting or praising the dead at the graves; the endpoint is included in the distraction.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī, al-Ālūsī, and Elmalılı explicitly include the endpoint. Ibn ʿĀshūr instead connects ḥattā to the utmost object counted, graves themselves."}, {"id": "102:2/q01/p3", "position": "The visit itself may end worldly greed by awakening the visitor.", "reasons": "Elmalılı allows this as a literal construal, while warning that reflection is not universal."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q02", "question": "Why is 'you visited' in the past tense?", "turns_on": "Whether the past form reports an actual past visit, vividly states a certain future, or addresses people from a later time.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q02/p1", "position": "The certain future is expressed as already completed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 16:1; al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı also allow the certainty of death."}, {"id": "102:2/q02/p2", "position": "The address includes people already dead or treats earlier generations as examples for the living.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares the Qur'anic address about earlier prophet-killers in 2:61; al-Ālūsī treats ancestral deaths as the listeners' own."}, {"id": "102:2/q02/p3", "position": "The addressees are already near death, so the grave is spoken of as reached.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives this reply to the objection that future death cannot be past."}, {"id": "102:2/q02/p4", "position": "God addresses unbelievers on Judgment Day, after their grave visit.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim proposes this; al-Ālūsī calls it astonishing, and Elmalılı says the next warning of future knowledge better fits this life or the grave."}, {"id": "102:2/q02/p5", "position": "The completed form presents a past tribal grave visit.", "reasons": "Paret takes the perfect as evidence of a historical episode; Corpus Coranicum favors the general gnomic statement."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q03", "question": "What does zurtum mean in Arabic usage?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase retains ordinary physical visiting, serves as the attested death idiom, or invokes the root's wider senses.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q03/p1", "position": "It means visiting or seeing a place without remaining there.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī likens a visit to going to water; Islahi cites a Ḥamāsī poem about revisiting one's land. Bint al-Shāṭi traces z-w-r to inclination and notes Qur'anic uses of ziyārah and tazāwar."}, {"id": "102:2/q03/p2", "position": "In poetry, visiting graves is an idiom for dying.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Ālūsī, Elmalılı and Bint al-Shāṭi cite Jarīr on Abū Mālik; al-Zamakhsharī also cites a year-end line, and Elmalılı cites al-Akhṭal."}, {"id": "102:2/q03/p3", "position": "The root can also express deviation or falsehood.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī notes zūr as forged handwriting; Bint al-Shāṭi relates the sensory idea of turning and cites 18:17, 22:30, 25:4, 25:72 and 58:2."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q04", "question": "What does visiting the graves mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse portrays death, an actual boastful trip, figurative mention of ancestors, or habitual boastful visits.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q04/p1", "position": "People remain absorbed in rivalry until they die and are buried.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr and Bint al-Shāṭi favor this. Jarīr and al-Akhṭal attest the death idiom; Ibn Kathīr cites a fever patient's saying that fever would send him to graves. Al-Rāzī answers the visitor objection by future departure for reckoning. Zayd b. Aslam's mursal report attributes to the Prophet an explanation of visiting the graves as the arrival of death."}, {"id": "102:2/q04/p2", "position": "They went physically to cemeteries and counted or praised their buried ancestors.", "reasons": "Reports locate the act in Quraysh or among Ansar. Al-Ālūsī calls the visit literal in the clan account; Ibn ʿĀshūr says grave stands for its occupant and cites al-Nābigha and a line variably attributed to ʿIṣām or Hammām. Al-Qurṭubī cites a poem of wealthy people continuing their boast through stone monuments at their graves."}, {"id": "102:2/q04/p3", "position": "Visiting is a figure for bringing the dead into the boast, whether or not the rivals actually went to the cemetery.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says it figuratively describes recollection; al-Bursawī calls it a euphemism; al-Ālūsī weighs metaphor, metonymy and representation, while al-Zamakhsharī calls it sarcastic. Abū Ḥayyān objects that this strains ordinary 'visit'."}, {"id": "102:2/q04/p4", "position": "The rebuke targets repeated cemetery visits made to advertise ancestors and one's visits.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes visits that crowd out worship and learning. Al-Ālūsī finds this reading remote, though he condemns boastful visits themselves."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q05", "question": "Why call burial a 'visit'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q05/p1", "position": "The grave is a temporary station before resurrection and a lasting home in Paradise or Hell.", "reasons": "A Bedouin and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz infer that a visitor must depart. Al-Rāzī uses departure for reckoning to answer the objection that the dead do not leave; al-Biqāʿī says even a long intermediate stay is short beside eternity. Bint al-Shāṭi includes reckoning and recompense."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q06", "question": "What does al-maqābir denote and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q06/p1", "position": "It is the plural of maqbara or maqbarah, a burial ground containing many graves.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās notes singular vowel variants and Hijazi usage; al-Qurṭubī distinguishes qubūr as plural of qabr and cites poetry and Abū Saʿīd al-Maqburī's name. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies land with many graves. Al-Qurṭubī distinguishes qabartu, 'I buried', from aqbartu, 'I ordered burial' (80:21)."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q07", "question": "Why use al-maqābir rather than qubūr?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural carries merely a lexical place sense or a distinctive collective image.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q07/p1", "position": "It evokes a vast collective cemetery across ages and social classes, fitting the end of accumulation.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭi and her Iʿjāz work prefer this semantic breadth over sound alone; the cadence also fits takāthur. Islahi notes the rhyme and the pity of the compressed journey to death. Al-Qurṭubī and Bint al-Shāṭi say maqābir occurs only here; Bint al-Shāṭi contrasts five uses of qubūr and singular qabr at 9:84."}, {"id": "102:2/q07/p2", "position": "It is treated simply as another word for graves or burial places.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭi argues this misses the collective setting and the swift movement from rivalry to death."}, {"id": "102:2/q07/p3", "position": "Al-maqābir is preferred to al-qubūr for its verbal harmony with the preceding takāthur.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭi's Iʿjāz account names verbal harmony in Sūrat al-Takāthur as the reason for this choice (102:1)."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q08", "question": "Who occasioned the warning by boasting at graves?", "turns_on": "Which transmitted setting is intended, and whether the verse is tied to a single contest or speaks generally.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q08/p1", "position": "Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Sahm of Quraysh counted living notables, then the dead; Sahm surpassed the other clan.", "reasons": "Reports differ in detail: some give a margin of three households; al-Bayḍāwī has Sahm invoke their pre-Islamic losses; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ also records the Meccan version, and Study Quran calls it best attested."}, {"id": "102:2/q08/p2", "position": "Jews boasted that their clans outnumbered one another and died astray.", "reasons": "Al-Qatāda is repeatedly cited for this view; some notes say rivalry distracted them from faith."}, {"id": "102:2/q08/p3", "position": "Two Ansar clans, Banū Ḥāritha and Banū al-Ḥārith, boasted of living then dead members.", "reasons": "Ibn Burayda names the clans; other reports merely say a clan among the Ansar. The naming and the generic Ansar formulation are variants of this occasion."}, {"id": "102:2/q08/p4", "position": "The warning describes recurrent tribal rivalry rather than one named occasion.", "reasons": "Qatada depicts one generation after another falling into graves. Al-Wāḥidī applies it to everyone distracted by rivalry; Kur'an Yolu says the general human target remains despite specific reports."}]}

"102:2/q09", "question": "Was the sūra revealed in Mecca or Medina?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported Ansar setting and related reports outweigh the common Meccan attribution.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q09/p1", "position": "It is Meccan, commonly dated after al-Kawthar.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr identifies it as Meccan; Abū Ḥayyān reports broad exegetical agreement, with al-Bukhārī as an exception. Bint al-Shāṭi gives the common sixteenth place in revelation."}, {"id": "102:2/q09/p2", "position": "It is Medinan.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers this from Ibn Burayda's Ansar occasion, a report from Ubayy, and ʿAlī's grave-punishment report; al-Bukhārī and a minority are also cited for Madinan attribution."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q10", "question": "Does the verse point to punishment in the grave?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q10/p1", "position": "Yes: the warning of knowledge upon reaching the graves implies punishment there.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Naḥḥās infer this; ʿAlī reportedly says Muslims doubted grave punishment until this sūra or its coming warning was revealed. Ibn Kathīr reports al-Tirmidhī grading ʿAlī's report gharīb. Al-Qurṭubī gives a view that they see God's punishment there; Elmalılı says hoarders awaken after losing their possessions."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q11", "question": "What conduct does the verse condemn when rivalry distracts people?", "turns_on": "Which goods are being pursued and whether the competition diverts from what truly matters.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q11/p1", "position": "Worldly boasting and accumulation divert people from obedience, faith, reflection and preparation for the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī names wealth and numbers; al-Rāzī ranks knowledge and virtue above bodily and external goods, citing Abraham's prayer in 26:83 and 57:20 on worldly rivalry. The range includes wealth, kin, allies, armies and pleasure. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies neglect of Qur'anic evidence and Islam's call; Asad extends the critique to consumerism, power, social disorientation and environmental damage. In a mursal report transmitted by Zayd b. Aslam, the Prophet specifies obedience as what rivalry in increase distracts people from."}, {"id": "102:2/q11/p2", "position": "Competition in knowledge, virtue and good deeds may be praiseworthy, whereas the familiar worldly rivalry is condemned.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the definite article identifies the blameworthy sort; competition in obedience may invite imitation, as 93:11 suggests. His example of al-ʿAbbās, Shayba and ʿAlī over good acts is linked to 9:19."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q12", "question": "What is the effect of leaving the object of distraction unstated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q12/p1", "position": "The omission widens and intensifies the rebuke to every religious duty displaced by rivalry.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī lists remembrance, obligations, recommended worship, knowledge, reflection and contemplation; al-Bayḍāwī says the suppressed object is religious concerns, and al-Ālūsī says the ambiguity magnifies blame. Zayd b. Aslam's mursal report gives the Prophet's expansion of the unstated object as obedience."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q13", "question": "How does this verse relate to the preceding and following warnings?", "turns_on": "Whether the note explains the lead-in from al-Qāriʿah or the transition to this sūra's following threat.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q13/p1", "position": "It recalls al-Qāriʿah: worldly numbers and wealth distract from the deeds weighed at Judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Ibn al-Zubayr connect preparation for the Calamity (101:1); Islahi says only deeds count in 101:6–11. Bint al-Shāṭi allows a shared warning tone in muṣḥaf order but rejects a revelation chronology link, since the sūras are separated by thirteen in that chronology. Elmalılı urges reflection on scales and destinations."}, {"id": "102:2/q13/p2", "position": "The clause leads to the next 'No indeed' and its afterlife threat.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says kallā rejects their accumulation, sawfa guarantees eventual knowledge, and the omitted object is its evil outcome; Elmalılı also reads the coming rebuke as a warning of what heedlessness will bring."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q14", "question": "What did the Prophet say endures when death ends rivalry?", "turns_on": "Which Prophetic saying is used to expose what remains valuable at death.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q14/p1", "position": "One's wealth is only what one consumes, wears out, or gives away in charity.", "reasons": "This saying follows recitation in al-Ṭabarī; al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Rāzī and al-Bursawī cite versions. Al-Thaʿlabī's Ibn ʿAbbās report defines takāthur as wrongful accumulation and withholding and names five blessings: food, drink, sleep, shade and health."}, {"id": "102:2/q14/p2", "position": "Family and wealth return from the burial, while the person's deeds remain.", "reasons": "Anas and Ibn Kathīr transmit the Prophet's report of three companions of the dead: family, wealth and deeds."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q15", "question": "What purpose should an actual grave visit serve?", "turns_on": "The visitor's intention and response: admonition and reform, or renewed pride and display.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q15/p1", "position": "It should remind visitors of death and the Hereafter, soften the heart and turn them toward good deeds.", "reasons": "The Prophet first forbade visits then permitted them for admonition in reports from ʿAlī, Abū Saʿīd, Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Hurayra; al-Tirmidhī grades Burayda's reminder report ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Al-Qurṭubī says direct sight is stronger than hearing, citing 'news is not like sight'; visiting is more accessible than witnessing death. Elmalılı compares a thoughtful visit to reading a book and says its best result is renewed resolve."}, {"id": "102:2/q15/p2", "position": "Visits made for boasting, display, or idle touring reverse that purpose and fall under the rebuke.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls their worldly attachment a reversal; ʿAlī says ancestral corpses should prompt humility. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān criticize monuments and shrines; Elmalılı points to wasteful display beside hungry neighbors."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q16", "question": "Are grave visits permitted or recommended?", "turns_on": "How the prohibition, later permission and this verse's rebuke apply to different motives for visiting.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q16/p1", "position": "Visits for remembrance are permitted, and some jurists call them recommended; the Prophet's later permission followed an earlier prohibition.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān cite the prophetic change. Elmalılı cites Dürr-i Muhtār for permissibility, including women; several Hanafi manuals recommend visits, and Radd al-Muḥtār recommends weekly visits on specified days. Elmalılı says the nonmutawātir report clarifies the verse's scope but cannot abrogate or restrict it."}, {"id": "102:2/q16/p2", "position": "The verse itself rebukes boastful visits, leaving reflective visits outside its condemnation.", "reasons": "Elmalılı defends this distinction against what he considers an overbroad reading of al-Ālūsī; he adds that promoting literal visits as the verse's central aim conflicts with the following rebuke."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q17", "question": "May women visit graves?", "turns_on": "Whether the curse precedes general permission and how grief, age and mixed gatherings affect visits.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q17/p1", "position": "The later general permission includes women as well as men.", "reasons": "Some scholars treat the curse report as predating permission; Dürr-i Muhtār permits women to visit. Al-Qurṭubī permits women when separated from men."}, {"id": "102:2/q17/p2", "position": "Women’s visits are disapproved or restricted, especially where grief or mixed gathering risks harm.", "reasons": "Al-Tirmidhī reports a curse on frequent female visitors and grades it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ; others cite women's lesser patience and greater grief. Al-Qurṭubī allows older women but not young women going out, while allowing any age when separated from men and forbidding tempting mixed gatherings."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q18", "question": "What should a visitor do at a grave?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q18/p1", "position": "Visit with a present heart; greet, pray, recite and reflect, while respecting the graves.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī prohibits walking or sitting on graves and says to approach known graves from the front. Elmalılı cites the Prophet at Baqīʿ, manuals recommending greeting, standing for prayer, reciting available Qur'an and sometimes approaching from the feet; reports vary about where the Prophet stood. {"id": "102:2/q21", "question": "Is the opening an assertion or an interrogative rebuke?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening carries an explicit interrogative hamza or reads as a statement.", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q21/p1", "position": "It is a declarative rebuke.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī calls the clause declarative and connects ḥattā to the continued distraction."}, {"id": "102:2/q21/p2", "position": "It may be read with an interrogative hamza, a question that asserts the rebuke.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reads the opening interrogatively; al-Rāzī cites analogous interrogative readings such as aʾ-andhartahum and aʾ-idhā kunnā ʿiẓāman."}]}
{"id": "102:2/q22", "question": "How is this sūra’s exceptional merit explained?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "102:2/q22/p1", "position": "Its thousand-verse merit has been explained as a sixth of the Qur'an because it addresses return to God.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Milq uses roughly 6,200 verses and al-Ghazālī's six aims; al-Ālūsī says the matter exceeds this calculation."}]}
{"id": "103:1/q01", "question": "What does al-ʿaṣr in the oath designate?", "turns_on": "Whether the unqualified word is inclusive or specifies a time of day, a prayer, a paired period, or a marked era; arguments use Arabic usage, poetry, report, context and analogous oaths.", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q01/p1", "position": "Time or an age broadly, encompassing its changing periods and events.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari declines restriction without textual proof; al-Nahhas and Elmalılı likewise allow several Arabic senses. Ibn Abbas and others identify an age; Imru al-Qays and Ibn al-Sikkit's poetry attest the usage. Farāhī and Asad distinguish fleeting ʿaṣr from dahr; Cuypers calls it a general span without further grounds. Ibn Kathir calls this the well-known view. Bint al-Shati follows al-Tabari, Ibn Qayyim and most exegetes; Kur'an Yolu finds this best suited to the sūra. Al-Razi questions treating a reported expanded wording as Qur'an because that would invalidate prayer. Elmalılı cites a poet likening unseen time's motion toward death to a ship. Al-Damghani glosses al-ʿaṣr as time or its passage; al-Suyuti includes time as a whole among the oath's possible referents. Al-Ṭabarī explicitly includes evening, night, and day without restricting the oath. Ibn Kathīr says this span contains human acts, good and evil."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p2", "position": "Late afternoon, the day's declining period from after noon toward sunset.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan and Qatada give the afternoon interval; al-Mawardi cites poetry, while Ibn Ashur defines it by shadow length and al-Harith ibn Hilliza's verse. The declining sun and approaching night signify divine power (Tabrisi, Nasafi, Qatada), and the closing market images judgment (Razi from Hasan). Robinson connects merchants' reckoning of earnings with verse 2's loss. Corpus Coranicum favors a specific daytime by analogy with other opening oaths, though observes late afternoon is unusual among early Meccan oaths. Ubayy's Prophetic report says God swears by day's end. Durr also reports Ibn Abbas and Qatada saying an hour of daytime; Tustari records 'afternoon or time itself'. Al-Suyuti also gives the day's latter part as the oath's referent. Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported to specify an unspecified daytime hour (al-Ṭabarī and al-Durr); Zayd b. Aslam calls it late afternoon or evening (Ibn Kathīr)."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p3", "position": "The afternoon prayer, the middle prayer distinguished by special merit.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls it the middle and best prayer. Hafsa's 2:238 recension and a reported reading of 5:106 are cited by Zamakhshari, Razi and others; Qurtubi cites an authentic identifying report. A Prophetic report likens missing it to losing family and property. Its hour conflicts with trade and livelihood, and Razi says it closes daily worship as repentance closes deeds. Razi also cites a report about a false oath after Asr and explains that God swears by His prescribed noble command. Alusi rejects Razi's sinful-woman story as unreliable. Neuwirth links prayer-time oaths to liturgical experience, though Corpus Coranicum disputes the proposed hymn tone. Al-Rāzī also invokes 5:106 as a scriptural argument for the afternoon prayer."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p4", "position": "The Prophet's era, honored by renewed prophethood and his community.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Qurtubi cite renewed prophethood. Razi and Elmalılı invoke the workers' parable: the final workers labor from Asr to sunset and receive double pay; compare oaths by the Prophet's place and life (90:2; 15:72). Elmalılı describes the mission, Hijra, victory, and extension of Muhammad's community to the end of time; the afternoon of human history follows earlier ages. Tabataba'i favors this because the next verses treat truth and perseverance. Bursevi cites a report of a day or half-day for the community and Najmiyya reports of the Prophet's primordial status. Al-Ālūsī cites al-Bukhārī's report comparing the Muslim community's remaining time with the interval from ʿAṣr to sunset. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the Islamic era because this sūra distinguishes responses after Islam's call; earlier peoples had unequal access to messengers."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p5", "position": "Night and day together, called the two ʿaṣrs.", "reasons": "Ibn Kaysan and others give the pair; Humayd ibn Thawr's poem uses the dual for day and night, as cited by Tha'labi, Wahidi, Qurtubi and others."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p6", "position": "The final hour of daytime, near sunset.", "reasons": "Qatada specifies the last hour, while Abu Muslim calls it one end of the day; this narrower reading is distinguished from the whole interval after noon."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p7", "position": "Morning and evening together, called the two ʿaṣrs.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Sikkit's and other poetic witnesses use the dual for morning and evening; Ibn Atiyya calls them the two cooler parts of day."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p8", "position": "The Lord of Time, implied as the object of the oath.", "reasons": "Baghawi cites comparable oaths and Qurtubi supplies the omitted 'Lord of the age'."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p9", "position": "The time of Adam's creation on Friday afternoon.", "reasons": "Biqai invokes a sound report in Muslim; Alusi reports this from Qatada. Elmalılı ties late creation to the world's closing day."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p10", "position": "Each person's lifetime, the finite capital in which one acts.", "reasons": "Biqai includes each individual life. Elmalılı's poems picture each passing day or breath consuming it; Islahi and Farāhī call it an investment whose melting-ice speed makes present duties urgent."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p11", "position": "The era of the Mahdi, when truth prevails fully.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i reports this from unnamed narrations."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p12", "position": "Time's vicissitudes or calamities.", "reasons": "Ali's interpretive recitation adds the vicissitudes of time and loss until its end; Jishumi reports this gloss but prefers time itself."}, {"id": "103:1/q01/p13", "position": "One unspecified member of either the day–night or the morning–evening pair.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī say that on the paired usages the singular oath can select either member without specifying which."}]}
{"id": "103:1/q02", "question": "What meanings and derivations does the word ʿaṣr have in Arabic?", "turns_on": "The sources distinguish its concrete pressing root, wide Arabic uses, bounded temporal force and the definite article's scope.", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q02/p1", "position": "Its root denotes squeezing or pressing, extended to time, confinement, and the extraction of an essence.", "reasons": "Jishumi describes wringing cloth, grape extract, deferred prayer, rain-bearing clouds and a rising dust column. Tabarsi applies the pressed-events image to time. Bint al-Shati adds press equipment, lineage and the hardship that presses out a person's essence; she cites 12:36, 12:49, 78:14 and 2:266. Biqai connects the sūra name to extracting the saved essence. Bint al-Shati reads human life as pressed and refined by trials, exposing its essence; she cites the root's occurrences in Yusuf's dream and harvest year and the whirlwind in al-Baqara, calls this Qur'anic form unique, and rejects al-Raghib's derivation of temporal ʿaṣr from what remains after squeezing. Her criticism of proposed links in other oaths cautions against assuming a simple analogy for this image."}, {"id": "103:1/q02/p2", "position": "The noun also spans an age, day or night, a part of day, prayer, group and rain.", "reasons": "Elmalılı adds Turkish senses of the current era and eighty or a hundred years and notes vocalizations ʿaṣr, ʿiṣr and ʿuṣr. Wahidi says these temporal senses are valid Arabic usage. Ibn ʿAṭiyya records variant vowel forms and distinguishes al-ʿaṣr for daytime from al-ʿashr for nighttime as reported by some scholars. Ibn ʿĀshūr lists eras named for a generation, ruler, prophet, or religion."}, {"id": "103:1/q02/p3", "position": "Unlike dahr's vast or unlimited duration, ʿaṣr marks a bounded, passing period.", "reasons": "Asad describes dahr as unbounded; Elmalılı cites Raghib's range from the universe's beginning to end, and Farāhī stresses swift passage, supported by Imru al-Qays and ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras. Bint al-Shati reports Razi's suggestion that 'asr avoids unbelievers' exalted dahr."}, {"id": "103:1/q02/p4", "position": "The word's definite article can be generic or point to a particular known time.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says the generic article can gather all senses while the covenant article directs the first hearers to their own era; Ibn Ash

{"id": "103:1/q03", "question": "How does the opening oath work, and what does it emphasize?", "turns_on": "Whether wāw is explained as a conventional emphatic oath or as time's witness to the proposition.", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q03/p1", "position": "The wāw introduces an oath whose answer affirms that humanity is in loss.", "reasons": "Jishumi identifies the oath particle and its answer; Elmalılı compares 93:1. Ibn Ashur says an oath confirms the assertion and its object displays God's creation, power and knowledge. Bint al-Shati says wāw magnifies what is sworn by and moves from perceptible reality to moral truth. Corpus Coranicum notes a possible pre-Islamic seer formula, a connection not yet studied adequately. Al-Zarkashi and al-Suyuti count oath openings as the fifth of the sūra-opening modes and list fifteen such sūras; al-Suyuti further classifies al-ʿAṣr as an oath followed by a proposition about human conduct or condition, namely humanity's loss. Al-Biqāʿī says the oath and emphatic answer announce that most people perish, a truth many deny in words or conduct."}, {"id": "103:1/q03/p2", "position": "Time itself bears witness to humanity's loss.", "reasons": "Islahi gives wāw this witness force: history shows recompense, while the rapidly spent lifespan makes a person's deeds profitable or ruinous."}, {"id": "103:1/q03/p3", "position": "A thematic link between an oath's object and its answer must be argued in each case, not assumed from other oaths.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati questions proposed links between night and day and differing human striving, and between the falling star and the Prophet's freedom from error; these analogies cannot by themselves establish the link in al-ʿAṣr."}]}
{"id": "103:1/q04", "question": "Why is time or afternoon singled out for the oath?", "turns_on": "The explanations appeal to divine signs, the day's closure, the prayer's status, the Prophet's era, historical recompense, or the value and moral use of time.", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q04/p1", "position": "Time displays divine power and wondrous changes, so its oath invites reflection.", "reasons": "Alternating nights and days, shifting light and temperature, health and illness, wealth and poverty, and other events disclose God's power (Razi, Ibn Qayyim, Tabarsi). Razi cites 25:62 and 6:13. Bursevi relates the oath to dawn, sun, moon, night, day and forenoon oaths. Ibn Ashur adds the solar-earth cycle and daily social life. Bint al-Shati cautions against loading the verse with speculative philosophy and cites 28:71–72. Al-Rāzī argues that time is nobler than place when reading 6:12–13; Ibn ʿĀshūr adds the changing atmosphere and God's creative artistry and knowledge."}, {"id": "103:1/q04/p2", "position": "Time is precious life capital; wasting it causes loss, while a final good act can gain lasting reward.", "reasons": "Mawardi cites the day's closing acts. Razi says a last moment of repentance can redeem a wasted life (25:62); al-Hasan compares closing markets to Judgment (21:1). Elmalılı cites elegies and poems about breath and passing days; Sufis urge afterlife-oriented use of the moment, while those denying afterlife seek worldly pleasure. Islahi and Farāhī compare time to melting ice and insist present obligations cannot be deferred. Al-Rāzī cites a poem exposing the paradox of rejoicing in passing days that shorten life; an early Muslim learned the sūra's point from an ice seller crying that his capital was melting."}, {"id": "103:1/q04/p3", "position": "The oath honors time and corrects blaming it for human misfortune.", "reasons": "Razi says Arabs blamed time; Elmalılı cites a poem saying people, not time, are corrupt, and 45:24 on materialists' dahr. Qashani and Bursevi cite 'do not revile time, for God is time'; Qashani says God, not time, acts through it. Muhammad Abdu posits blameworthy afternoon talk, but Bint al-Shati rejects a special gathering hour because talk can occur at any time."}, {"id": "103:1/q04/p4", "position": "Afternoon closes work and gathers gains, picturing final reckoning and death.", "reasons": "Biqai sees the end of work and beginning of rest; Razi's Abu Muslim pairs morning's resurrection signs with evening's death signs, and his al-Hasan likens it to closing markets. Al-Nisaburi urges a trade without loss before sunset; Robinson links merchants' daily reckoning to verse 2. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes the closing of field and market work, return to family, and divinely inspired daily work rhythms."}, {"id": "103:1/q04/p5", "position": "The afternoon prayer's difficulty and merit make its mention an exhortation to observe it.", "reasons": "The cited middle-prayer readings and missing-prayer report support its rank. Razi says God magnifies a prescribed command, and Alusi objects to the story of the sinful woman. Al-Rāzī adds 5:106, reports a warning against a false oath after ʿAṣr, and argues that God swears by a noble command He instituted. Ibn ʿĀshūr also reports a false sales oath after the prayer."}, {"id": "103:1/q04/p6", "position": "The Prophetic era is the decisive setting in which truth appeared and rejection became especially grave.", "reasons": "Razi uses the last workers' double wage and compares oaths by the Prophet's place and life; Elmalılı traces his mission, revelation, victory and continuing community. Tabataba'i invokes the following verses on truth and patience. Ibn ʿĀshūr favors the Islamic era because the sūra judges those reached by Islam's call, unlike earlier peoples whose access to messengers varied."}, {"id": "103:1/q04/p7", "position": "Past peoples' histories bear witness to God's law of recompense.", "reasons": "Farāhī says virtue gained ascendancy and oppression led to destruction after respite; their past eras urge belief and action before time passes."}, {"id": "103:1/q04/p8", "position": "Time presses and refines people through hardship, exposing their worth as the following verses distinguish loss from salvation.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati connects the pressing sense of ʿaṣr to humanity's trials and to the next verses' account of loss and rescue."}]}
{"id": "103:1/q05", "question": "How is al-ʿaṣr read?", "turns_on": "Whether the transferred kasra is confined to pause or transmitted in connected recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q05/p1", "position": "The received reading keeps ṣād vowelless in pause; Salām's reading gives ṣād kasra by vowel transfer.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya limits Salām's al-ʿaṣri and al-ṣabri to pause; Razi attributes the sound to breath or another impediment. Abu al-Fadl says transfer marks inflection and avoids two vowelless letters; Samīn gives poetic examples and also ḍamma transfer. A rajaz line in fī al-ʿaṣr supports the form."}, {"id": "103:1/q05/p2", "position": "Reports also allow the kasra in connected recitation.", "reasons": "Al-Hudhali transmits Abu ʿAmr routes for al-ʿaṣr, al-ṣabr, al-fajr and al-watr in pause and liaison; Ibn Khalawayh does not restrict al-ṣabri to pause. Samīn records an imāla-like variant on bāʾ."}]}
{"id": "103:1/q06", "question": "What expanded recitations of the verse are reported?", "turns_on": "Whether the additions are transmitted interpretations or canonical text, and which expanded wording is attributed to whom.", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q06/p1", "position": "Ali's recitation names the vicissitudes of time and extends human loss until time's end.", "reasons": "Tabari, Tha'labi and Elmalılı transmit the interpretive expansion with time's calamities; Razi refuses to treat an expanded report as Qur'anic wording because it would invalidate prayer."}, {"id": "103:1/q06/p2", "position": "A recitation attributed to Ali and Ibn Masʿud adds loss until time's end without naming vicissitudes.", "reasons": "Tha'labi gives both attributions; the wording differs from his other Ali report. {"id": "103:1/q09", "question": "How does this opening connect with other Qur'anic passages?", "turns_on": "The links draw on the preceding sūra, analogous oaths, parallels to the exception, and the sūra's own later clauses.", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q09/p1", "position": "It follows al-Takāthur by exposing the loss caused by worldly distraction.", "reasons": "Jishumi says the prior warning against abundance leads to the demand for deeds; Abu Hayyan distinguishes believer and unbeliever. Biqai and Alusi continue the warning of 102; Study Quran cites 102:1 and 102:8 about wasted time and accountable blessings."}, {"id": "103:1/q09/p2", "position": "It complements oaths by the forenoon and other day and night phases.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Nasafi and others pair afternoon with 93:1; Razi contrasts prior midmorning rising fortunes with afternoon decline. Bursevi cites oaths in 89, 91, 92 and 93; Corpus Coranicum observes this afternoon oath is unusual among early Meccan oaths."}, {"id": "103:1/q09/p3", "position": "The exception here adds mutual counsel to faith and works mentioned elsewhere.", "reasons": "Samarrai says counsel in truth and patience prevents further loss of reward."}, {"id": "103:1/q09/p4", "position": "A verse about protected life uses this sūra as a parallel for a generic statement with an exception.", "reasons": "Qurtubi compares the generic definite al-nafs and its legally qualified exception to generic human statements in 103:1–3, citing 70:19 and 70:22."}, {"id": "103:1/q09/p5", "position": "Its message distinguishes those saved from those ruined, framing the whole sūra.", "reasons": "Biqai maps the clauses to knowledge of God and afterlife, worship, doubt and patience, and says preventing harm precedes benefit. Bint al-Shati links the opening's pressing image to the later contrast between human loss and salvation."}, {"id": "103:1/q09/p6", "position": "The oath by this age parallels oaths by the Prophet's life and the city where he lived.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr compare 15:72 and 90:2 to explain why the Prophet's era is honored."}, {"id": "103:1/q09/p7", "position": "After al-Takāthur, it shows the state of those whom rivalry in abundance did not distract.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī connects the previous sūra's warning with the successful people described here."}]}
{"id": "103:1/q10", "question": "Was the sūra revealed in Mecca or Medina?", "turns_on": "The authorities' differing attributions; the notes supply no decisive historical test.", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q10/p1", "position": "It was revealed in Mecca.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr and most authorities support Mecca (Abu Hayyan, Alusi); Tabataba'i says it seems more likely Meccan, while Study Quran also reports this. Al-Suyuti cites al-Bayhaqi's transmission from Ikrima and al-Hasan naming al-ʿAṣr among the Meccan sūras."}, {"id": "103:1/q10/p2", "position": "It was revealed in Medina.", "reasons": "Mawardi cites one narration from Ibn Abbas and Qatada; Abu Hayyan and Alusi add Mujahid and Muqatil. {"id": "103:1/q11", "question": "How many verses does the sūra have, and where is its first break?", "turns_on": "The position of the first verse boundary; the reported total count is three.", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q11/p1", "position": "It has three verses, with the oath as its own first verse.", "reasons": "Alusi calls the three-verse count undisputed; Neuwirth favors an independent oath in line with other openings. Al-Zarkashi counts al-ʿAṣr as a one-word opening verse by analogy with al-Fajr and al-Ḍuḥā and their rhyme despite different lengths, and notes that a single utterance can form a verse. Al-Suyuti reports scholars adding wa-l-ʿaṣr to standalone verses; the counters other than the later Medinans count this opening separately."}, {"id": "103:1/q11/p2", "position": "Medina II joins the oath to verse 2 in its division.", "reasons": "Spitaler reports this verse division. Al-Suyuti reports that the later Medinan count instead makes wa-tawāṣaw bi-l-ḥaqq a separate verse while all still total three. Al-Mawsili's scheme distinguishes disagreements in internal breaks from disagreements in totals."}, {"id": "103:1/q11/p3", "position": "Under Abu ʿAmr al-Dani's one-word rule, wa-l-ʿaṣr would not form a standalone verse.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti reports al-Dani's assertion that mudhāmmatān is the only word that constitutes an āya on its own; the report does not itself supply an alternative three-verse division for al-ʿAṣr."}]}
{"id": "103:1/q12", "question": "When in the revelation sequence did this sūra come?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q12/p1", "position": "It followed shortly after Sūra 94.", "reasons": "Asad states this; Study Quran calls the sequence likely. {"id": "103:1/q13", "question": "What does the sūra as a whole teach?", "turns_on": "The notes differ in emphasis between the sūra's moral summary, its extraction imagery, decline, and inward lessons.", "positions": [{"id": "103:1/q13/p1", "position": "It compresses the Qur'an's path of salvation: faith, good works, truth and patience avert universal loss.", "reasons": "Muhammad ibn Kaʿb says belief alone does not suffice; the four qualities follow in order. Sulami lists neglect of God's rights, desires and lack of fear as causes of loss. Qutb calls the sūra a concise Muslim constitution, while Biqai relays Ghazali's six Qur'anic themes and maps the clauses to them. Al-Shafi'i says reflection on this sūra would suffice; Akif's poem repeats its sequence. Ibn ʿĀshūr includes patiently purifying oneself and inviting others to truth, and reports that the sūra encompasses all Qur'anic sciences."}, {"id": "103:1/q13/p2", "position": "Its imagery extracts the enduring saved essence from transient worldly life.", "reasons": "Biqai explains the name through extraction, describes the doomed and saved, and reads the basmala as contrasting perishing things with God's enduring mercy."}, {"id": "103:1/q13/p3", "position": "Each generation falls below its predecessor unless it follows the saving path.", "reasons": "Study Quran applies the decline reading both to individuals and to human history."}, {"id": "103:1/q13/p4", "position": "Affliction drives God's servants toward Him and falls on the spiritually best first.", "reasons": "Qashani describes affliction as God's whip and ranks prophets, saints and others by the order of its incidence."}, {"id": "103:1/q13/p5", "position": "Hearing, knowing and accompanying God's name call for wealth, self and spirit to be given to it.", "reasons": "Qushayri says hearing yields generosity, knowing ends preference for self, and companionship gives eternal life and the spirit's surrender."}]}
